explain.say: Share! Look at this reason. Each atom puts in one electron, and the pair sits between them, held by both nuclei. That shared pair is a covalent bond, and it is very strong. How many electrons do you think are in one covalent bond?

explain.say: Two! Now look at the molecules on the board. A molecule is a group of atoms joined by covalent bonds. Water, H2O, has two single bonds. Methane, the gas in many cookers, has a carbon sharing with four hydrogens. Can you count its bonds?

Four! Brilliant, you are thinking like a chemist. Some atoms share two pairs, a double bond, like oxygen gas and carbon dioxide. Nitrogen shares three pairs! Wow: that triple bond is so strong that nitrogen, 78 percent of the air, hardly reacts at all.

faq.a: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Both nuclei are attracted to the shared pair, which holds the atoms together.

faq.q: Why do non-metal atoms share electrons?
faq.a: Both atoms need extra electrons to fill their outer shells, so neither will give electrons away. By sharing pairs, each can count the shared electrons as its own.
asks: Why do atoms form covalent bonds?

faq.a: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds, like water, H2O, or oxygen, O2.
A double bond is two shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms. Oxygen gas, O=O, and carbon dioxide, O=C=O, have double bonds.

faq.q: Why does water boil so easily if covalent bonds are strong?
faq.a: The covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong, but the forces between separate molecules are much weaker. Boiling only overcomes those weak forces between molecules.
asks: Why do simple molecules have low melting points?

facts: A single covalent bond is one shared pair of electrons; a double bond is two shared pairs.
Nitrogen gas, N2, has a triple bond, one of the strongest bonds between two atoms.
